_readme: Mutation evidence a target's acceptance quotes, kept executable (🎯T32).
A target's acceptance says 'reintroducing X makes test T RED'. That sentence
is quoted once, in a commit message, and then never re-run. Any later commit
that changes T's inputs can retire the evidence without turning anything red:
🎯T30's 8c5e04a added a `landed` argument to ensureSubmitted and passed
landed=true at 🎯T28's call sites, which was correct for the branch it modelled
and weakened no assertion — but it made 🎯T28's over-broadness mutation stop
biting TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess. Every suite stayed green.
This file is the machine-readable form of those sentences, and
scripts/check-mutation-evidence.py re-derives them: `make verify-mutation-evidence`,
run in CI. Each entry names the target, the mutation as an anchored source edit,
and the tests that must go RED (and the ones that must stay GREEN) under it.
The same Makefile target also runs the check with --prove-teeth, which is what
keeps THIS check from becoming the next unwired oracle: an entry may declare a
`decay`, and --prove-teeth asserts that applying it leaves every suite green
(so CI sees nothing) while making a `red` test survive the mutation (so this
check, and only this check, goes red).
TO ADD AN ENTRY when you quote mutation evidence in a commit body:
target    the target whose acceptance quotes it
mutation  a stable id for this mutation, unique within the target
what      one line: what the mutation reintroduces or removes
quoted_by the commit whose message quotes this evidence
package   the Go package the tests live in
edits     [{file, find, replace}] — `find` must occur EXACTLY ONCE in file.
Anchor text, not a diff hunk: a hunk decays on the first refactor
of its context. When the anchor stops matching the check goes RED
and says so, which is the point — the mutation must be re-derived
by a human, never silently skipped.
tests     [{name, expect}] — name is a `go test` path, so a subtest is
'TestX/subtest_name'. expect is 'red' (the mutation must kill it)
or 'green' (it must survive — that is how a commit body's
'fixture Y stays green under this mutation, so the two cover
distinct mechanisms' claim stays true).
decay     optional {what, models, edits} — an edit to the TESTS' inputs,
modelled on a real commit, that disarms this evidence without
turning any suite red. --prove-teeth applies it and requires
exactly that: green everywhere on its own, and a `red` test
surviving the mutation once both are applied. Worth declaring
for any entry whose evidence has decayed once already.
note      optional prose: provenance, or what decayed here before.

entries.what: Agent.Send drops the provider's error and returns nil, the swallow that made a lost submit invisible above agent.go
entries.note: 2017074 also quoted TestClaudeSendReportsUnsubmittedTurnThroughRealTmux against this mutation. It is not listed here because it skips without tmux and a skipped test is not evidence; the hermetic one holds the contract in every environment.

entries.what: MatchTurnInProgress forgets Claude Code's activity line, so a running turn with a drained composer reads as no chrome at all

decay.what: the Send-level call site passes landed=true, so sawContent starts true and 🎯T30's composerEmptyIdle branch returns nil before the 🎯T28 classification is consulted at all
decay.models: 8c5e04a, which did this to TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess: correct for the paste branch that test models, no assertion weakened, every suite green, and the caller-visible half of 🎯T28's evidence gone

edits.find: if err := ensureSubmitted(d, false); err != nil {
edits.replace: if err := ensureSubmitted(d, true); err != nil {

entries.note: This is the entry 🎯T32 was filed over. aa71680 quoted TestT28DailyDeliveredFramesReportSuccess/frame_daily_spinner_empty_composer.txt as the caller-visible RED half. 8c5e04a passed landed=true at that call site and the subtest went green under the mutation, leaving only the classifier half biting; 9944f39 restored the contract on the landed=false path as TestT28DeliveredFramesReportSuccessWithoutLandedEvidence, which is what this entry names. The green expectation is aa71680's own distinctness claim: the queued frame is the half 2017074 already closed, so the two fixtures cover different mechanisms rather than doubling up.

entries.what: classifyComposer forgets Claude Code's queued-messages hint, so a payload accepted behind a running turn stops counting as submitted
MatchUnsubmittedPaste asks whether the composer was DRAWN rather than whether it HOLDS anything, the pre-fix predicate that reported delivered sends as stuck chips
maybeContinueGoal stops calling Send, so an open Goal dies after one terminal turn
TestHermeticTaskRunSuccess bounds its run with a 10s context deadline again — the wall-clock bound that let a loaded machine, not the product, decide the verdict

edits.replace:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10000000000)
	defer cancel()
	events, err := task.Run(ctx, "summarize")

entries.note: The deadline is spelled as a bare 10000000000 so the mutation needs no new import; the guard matches the context.WithTimeout call, not the literal. TestHermeticTaskRunSuccess is listed green on purpose: on an idle machine the restored deadline still passes, which is exactly why this flake stayed citable-green between failures and why the guard, not the test, holds the contract.

entries.what: WaitForResponse arms no silence wake at all, so a turn whose terminal event never arrives has nothing to end it — the unbounded park itself
entries.note: The red test is structural on purpose. A missing wake is invisible to a behavioural test — it shows up as a HANG, which is the original defect's own signature and costs a test timeout to see (the report that opened 🎯T96 was a 10m panic). Arming the wake before the subscription gives the guard a happens-before point, so the absence is a fast failure instead of a dead suite. The green test is load-bearing: the death wake is a separate mechanism and still answers with no silence timer on the clock at all.

entries.what: markDead records the death but closes nothing, so the alive flag flips where no waiter can see it and a wait on that agent keeps waiting for an event nothing will publish
entries.note: TestWaitForResponseEndsWhenTheAgentDies fails FAST under this mutation rather than hanging, and that is by design: it drives the clock past its own bound, so an unobserved death is reported as ErrTurnAbandoned — the wrong verdict, available in milliseconds — instead of parking. The green test shows the silence bound cannot cover for the death wake: it never involves a live agent, so it is blind to this mutation.

entries.what: the wait counts only published events as turn activity, so a tmux turn that is plainly working — the TUI repainting its spinner — is convicted as silent because its tool call wrote nothing to the transcript
entries.note: The two activity sources are independent claims and this pins them apart: events still rearm the bound under this mutation, so the green test cannot see it. A bound that only watched the transcript would fire on exactly the longest healthy turns — a Claude tool call emits no JSONL between tool_use and tool_result, however long the tool runs.

entries.what: WaitForResponse goes back to subscribing for future events only, so the turn a blocking submit has already consumed is dropped on the floor — the park that took the root package's 10m alarm
entries.note: The mutation is the differential run that identified 🎯T98: the handover disabled, everything else — the latch, the arming in Send, the recording in publishEvent — left in place, so what goes red is the handover and nothing else. TestWaitForResponseIgnoresEventsFromBeforeTheSubmit is declared green on purpose: it holds the other half of the contract, that the latch never hands back a turn from before the submit, and a mutation that simply deleted the latch would satisfy it trivially. It staying green is what makes the red ones evidence about the handover rather than about the latch existing at all.

entries.what: the read loop names the oversized frame but abandons the stream mid-line, so the next read returns the tail of that frame instead of the next message — the 🎯T661 defect with a better error message

edits.replace:
case len(line)+len(chunk) > MaxLineLen:
			return nil, frameTooLarge(len(line) + len(chunk))

entries.note: The green test is load-bearing, not decoration: it never crosses the cap, so it stays green under this mutation and shows the red ones are pinning the skip specifically, not any breakage of the reader. The red tests overshoot the cap by 3x MaxLineLen on purpose. An earlier fixture overshot by 7 bytes and this mutation SURVIVED it, because a frame that exceeds the cap inside the final read buffer is consumed to its terminator by the read that notices — a false green the sizes now exclude.

entries.what: EncodeEventWire marshals the event without bounding it, so a screenshot tool_result is handed to the wire as a frame over the line cap — the producer half of the same incident
entries.note: The green test holds the other half of the contract: an unbounded codec still relays an ordinary event byte for byte, so it cannot distinguish the two codecs and the red tests are what pin the bound.

entries.what: bounding treats its own conservative budget as the wire's cap: a payload over the budget with nothing long enough to elide is relayed with Raw set to nil, although the frame it would have produced is legal — data thrown away to protect a limit that was never in danger

edits.find:
ev.Raw, ev.Text = raw, text
	ev.Truncated = ev.Truncated || rawCut || textCut

entries.note: This is the defect the adopted branch shipped with, and the two green tests are why it survived its own suite: every other fixture in broker_bound_test.go carries a base64 string far over maxWireStringBytes, so elision always reaches it and the discard branch is never taken. Only a payload whose size is in its shape — hundreds of small strings, none of them long — lands in the gap between the budget (MaxLineLen/2) and the frame ceiling, and there the bound deleted a payload the wire would have carried. The second green test holds the other side of the same boundary: past the ceiling with nothing elidable, dropping Raw is still the right answer, so the red test is pinning where the line sits and not whether there is one.
